newsitem.title: USA: Democratic Cuba would get billions of dollars -U.S..
newsitem.headline: Democratic Cuba would get billions of dollars -U.S..

text.p: The United States dangled the prospect of billions of dollars in loans and investment before Cuba on Tuesday, saying the money could be Havana's if it embraced democracy and dumped Fidel Castro.

The White House released a document with a preface written by President Bill Clinton that outlined how the United States and others would help Cuba if the Communist-ruled country joined the ranks of "prosperous democratic nations."

"It is reasonable to project that during a six year period following the establishment of a transition government, Cuba would receive from $4 billion to $8 billion from the international financial institutions, multilateral organisations and individual countries," the report said.

Cuba also could expect to attract more than one billion dollars anually from its expatriates in the United States -- once Washington lifts limits on money transfers -- as well as hundreds of millions of dollars in foreign direct investment.
The plan, drafted by the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID), did not predict when or how a transition might take place in the only communist country in the Americas.
It describes what financial needs would arise if Cuba were to take the path followed by Eastern European nations after the fall of the Berlin Wall.

"This is an assessment of what we believe the areas of assistance will be, not that these are the areas of assistance that we are imposing," USAID assistant administrator Mark Schneider told reporters.
A democratizing Cuba would have advantages that other former Soviet bloc nations had not had, including strong U.S. interest in having a democratic neighbour, the report said.

"The amount of available financing, official and private, for Cuba's transition appears to be quite large, certainly larger than what was available on a per capita basis to any of the countries of the former Soviet Union," it said.
But the prerequisite political changes would be dramatic.

The report said such assistance would be available to a Cuban "transition government", which is defined under the Helms-Burton law passed last year as a government that does not include either Fidel Castro or his brother Raul.

A transition Cuban government also would have to legalise all political activity, release all political prisoners, dissolve the Cuban Department of State Security, and commit to organising elections within 18 months, among other things.
The White House issued the report to comply with the Helms-Burton law, which is officially named the Cuban Liberty and Democratic Solidarity Act.

The document appeared to offer concrete incentives to Cubans to change, in contrast with punitive anti-Castro measures -- such as the economic embargo enforced since 1962 -- long employed by Washington.
The Helms-Burton law tightened the U.S. embargo by seeking to deter investment on the island through threats to punish foreign firms that benefit from property seized under Castro.
Clinton signed the law in March, shortly after Cuban MiG fighter jets shot down two small U.S. civilian aircraft, killing four men from a Miami anti-Castro group.

But faced with mounting opposition to the measure from U.S. allies, Clinton has postponed a controversial provision that would allow U.S. citizens to sue foreigners investing in their confiscated properties in Cuba.
The report said the U.S. embargo would be lifted if Cuba moved toward democracy.
The report also listed Cuba's advantages over the former Soviet bloc countries that abandoned their controlled economies in favour of market-based policies.

"As Cuba has already undergone the shock from the collapse of COMECON trade, the adjustment period for Cuba following commencement of sustained economic liberalisation is likely to be shorter than that experienced by other former Soviet bloc countries," it said. COMECON was the Soviet-led trading bloc.
The U.S. sanctions hardly hobbled Cuba while the Soviet Union was its main ally. But after Soviet communism crumbled in 1991, the island's economy plummeted.
Since then Castro has been trying to attract badly needed investment by opening up key economic sectors such as tourism, mining and telecommunications to foreign partners.
